summary: Adds a Connection ID (CID) to DTLS 1.2. Normally a DTLS receiver identifies a session by the sender's address and port, which breaks if those change mid-session, for example after a network switch or a NAT rebinding. With a CID in the record header, the receiver can still find the right security context. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Your name tag stays the same even if you change seats, so people can still tell who you are.

questions: dtls session after ip address change
how does cid work in dtls 1.2
subtitle: A connection identifier in the DTLS 1.2 record header, so a session survives a change of IP address or port.

tldr.problem: DTLS 1.2 finds the right security context from the sender's 5-tuple. If the source address or port changes mid-session, for example after NAT rebinding, the receiver cannot find the session and a costly new handshake is needed.
tldr.mechanism: Both sides negotiate a connection_id extension in the hello messages. Afterwards each encrypted record carries the CID the receiver asked for, in a new record format with content type tls12_cid(25), a changed MAC computation, an encrypted real content type and optional padding.
tldr.outcome: The receiver can look up the session by CID, while strict rules on peer address updates limit spoofing and replay. The RFC warns that the CID adds linkability and that DTLS 1.2 has no CID update, so DTLS 1.3 is preferred where that matters.

today: RFC 9146 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6347, and it is itself updated by RFC 9853. The text points to a separate DTLS 1.3 specification for carrying the CID in DTLS 1.3 and encourages developers to switch to that version.

sections.title: Why DTLS Needs a Connection ID
sections.content:
RFC 6347 defines DTLS, which secures data sent over datagram transports such as UDP. Like TLS, it starts with a handshake that can be computationally demanding, and then uses symmetric cryptography for the rest of the session. The idea is to spread the cost of the handshake over a long period of protected traffic.

In DTLS as specified in RFC 6347, the IP address and port of the peer identify the association. In some cases, such as NAT rebinding, these values are not enough. The RFC calls this a particular issue in the Internet of Things, where devices enter extended sleep periods to save battery. A rebinding then causes a connection failure and the cost of a new handshake.

This document adds a Connection ID (CID) to the DTLS 1.2 record layer, negotiated through a DTLS extension. Because the record format changes anyway, it also encrypts the record type and allows padding, following TLS 1.3 practice. The RFC updates RFC 6347.
sections.eli5: Usually a computer knows who is talking by looking at where the message came from. If that address changes, it gets confused. A connection ID is a label inside the message, so it still knows who is talking.

sections.title: The connection_id Extension
sections.content:
The connection_id extension (type 54) is carried in the ClientHello and ServerHello. Its data is a ConnectionId structure holding an opaque value of 0 to 2^8-1 bytes. Each side puts in the CID that it wants to receive. The client's value is what it wants the server to use when sending to the client, and the server's reply holds the CID it wants the client to use.

A zero-length value has a special meaning. A client that sends one is prepared to send using a CID but does not want the server to use one. A server that replies with a zero-length value will send using the client's CID but does not want the client to include one. So a CID can be used in one direction only.

Because each party chooses the value it receives, an implementation can use a constant length for its CIDs, which eases parsing. It must still be able to send CIDs of other lengths. If it wants variable-length CIDs, it must build them so the length can be determined on reception, since the record does not carry the length.

CIDs are exchanged only at the start of the session. DTLS 1.2 has no CID update message, and a resumed or renegotiated session negotiates the extension afresh.

If no CID was negotiated, or a zero-length CID was advertised for a direction, the RFC 6347 record format MUST be used in that direction. With a non-zero CID, once encryption is enabled, records MUST use the new format with content type tls12_cid.

On receipt, the tls12_cid content type means the CID is used to look up the connection and security association. Otherwise the lookup uses the 5-tuple, and if a non-zero CID was expected for that association, the datagram MUST be treated as invalid.
sections.eli5: Each side tells the other what name tag it wants to see on messages sent to it. If you say your tag is blank, you are saying you will wear a tag for them but they need not wear one for you.

sections.title: The CID-Enhanced Record Format
sections.content:
Records that use a CID have the distinguished content type tls12_cid, value 25. It has three implications: the CID field is present and has one or more bytes, the MAC is calculated as described in the next section, and the real content type is inside the encryption envelope.

Plaintext records are not affected, so the DTLSPlaintext structure is unchanged. For protected records, the content is first wrapped with its real type and optional padding into a DTLSInnerPlaintext: the content, then real_type, then a run of zero bytes. The zeros let a sender pad a record by a chosen amount, within record size limits, as in TLS 1.3.

That structure is encrypted, and the CID is added to form the DTLSCiphertext. Its outer type is always tls12_cid, followed by version, epoch, sequence number, the cid, the length and the encrypted content. The receiver finds the real type only after decryption. If CIDs of different lengths are in use, they must be self-delineating, because nothing else tells the receiver which connection, and therefore which CID length, applies.
sections.eli5: The real label for what is inside the envelope is hidden inside it. On the outside there is only a plain stamp saying a connection ID is present, followed by the name tag.

sections.title: Record Payload Protection
sections.content:
The MAC calculation and, for AEAD ciphers, the additional data differ for records with content type tls12_cid. The modified algorithm MUST NOT be applied to records that carry no CID. The RFC defines the fields cid, cid_length, length_of_DTLSInnerPlaintext (which MUST NOT exceed 2^14) and seq_num_placeholder, which is 8 bytes of 0xff.

Three variants are given. Block ciphers without Encrypt-then-MAC and block ciphers with it get a new MAC input, and AEAD ciphers get a changed additional-data input. All of them start with the placeholder, the tls12_cid type and the CID length, and then feed in the version, epoch, sequence number and CID.

The rationale is to keep the MAC input for DTLS without a CID separate from the input with one. The old form starts with a sequence number followed by a content type other than tls12_cid, and the new form always starts with the placeholder followed by tls12_cid. The epoch and sequence number are now also fed in the order they appear on the wire.
sections.eli5: The secret check code now includes the name tag, and it is built in a different way, so a code made for a tagged message can never be mistaken for one made for an untagged message.

sections.title: Updating the Peer Address
sections.content:
When a record with a CID arrives from a source address different from the one currently associated with the connection, the receiver MUST NOT replace the address it sends to unless three conditions are met.

  • The datagram has been cryptographically verified by the normal DTLS record processing.
  • It is newer, in both epoch and sequence number, than the newest datagram received. This stops reordered old datagrams from reverting a valid change and limits an attacker's ability to force a spurious change by replaying datagrams.
  • There is a strategy for ensuring the new address can receive and process DTLS records. The RFC mandates none, but suggests an application-level check, such as a small ping-pong exchange, or a DTLS-specific mechanism as described in the draft it cites.

The RFC does not require the anti-replay window from RFC 6347. Either the window or the newer-than-latest rule prevents address updates from replay attacks. A datagram that passes verification but triggers no address change is still a valid record and goes to the application. Records with bad MACs or that are otherwise invalid MUST be silently discarded.
sections.eli5: If a letter arrives from a new return address, you only start writing back to that new address after checking the letter is real, that it is newer than your last letter, and that someone really lives there.

sections.title: Example Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC's example shows a CID used in one direction only, from client to server. The client sends connection_id=empty, meaning it will not receive a CID, and the server answers with connection_id=100. After the handshake reaches encryption, the client's records carry CID=100.

In DTLS 1.2 only one handshake message is encrypted, the Finished message. So in this example only the client's Finished and the application data it sends include a CID. Server-to-client records use the old format because the client asked for no CID.
sections.eli5: The server gives the client a name tag, number 100. The client wears it on its secret messages, but the server wears none, so only one side labels its messages.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The CID replaces the 5-tuple as an identifier that persists for the whole connection, and any identifier brings a risk of linkability. An on-path observer can link all payloads that carry the same ID pair. Without multihoming or mobility, the CID exposes the same information as the 5-tuple. With multihoming, a passive attacker can correlate traffic over the two paths. Because DTLS 1.2 has no CID update mechanism, the RFC says the extension is unsuitable for mobility scenarios where correlation matters, and such deployments SHOULD refuse CIDs in DTLS 1.2 and use DTLS 1.3, which has a CID update and sequence number encryption.

On the positive side, the new record format brings padding, which inflates ciphertext size and makes traffic analysis harder. Endpoints can also use the CID to attach arbitrary per-connection metadata to records, which could inform on-path observers. Implementations concerned about this SHOULD refuse to use CIDs.

For security, an on-path adversary can mount reflection attacks against third parties because a peer cannot tell a genuine address change from a malicious one. This matters most when the request is small and the response large. An attacker who sees the traffic can also replay datagrams with modified addresses or ports, which is why the address update rules in the previous section matter.
sections.eli5: A name tag that never changes lets people watching you tell it is the same you every time. If that matters, use the newer version, which can change the tag.
